look_here_first: FIND THE WINTER ROSETTE, THEN MEASURE A SPIKELET: a perennial tuft often makes a broad-leaved basal rosette. Spring panicles are open; spikelets are comparatively LARGE for this set, often about 2.9–4 mm long. Inspect the fringe-like hair ligule and whether long hairs arise from small bumps on the sheath.

best_field_traits: Basal winter rosette of shorter, broader blades; spring flowering culms and autumn secondary branches can look dramatically different.
Open spring panicle commonly about 4–13 cm long; later branch heads can be small and partly sheathed.
Lance-shaped stem blades often 3–14 cm long and 3–12 mm wide.
Ligule fringe of hairs about 1–4.2 mm long in broad treatments.
Sheaths range from nearly smooth to coarse hairy, sometimes with raised tubercle/pustule bases; avoid identifying from sheath hair alone.
Mature spikelets commonly 2.9–4 mm; lower glume is shorter than entire spikelet.
crew_field_check: Start from the same rooted clump; note spring vs late-season growth.
Expose the collar and photograph the true ligule with a ruler; separate the blade-base cilia from collar hairs.
Measure at least three mature spikelets and examine glumes under magnification.
If collar or spikelet anatomy is absent, label as provisional Dichanthelium sp.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: collar ligule in side view with mm scale

confused_with: other Dichanthelium species (not yet represented in this learner)
comparisons.key_distinctions: Much larger spikelets than D. lindheimeri are helpful. D. pedicellatum can overlap in spikelet length; check its usually narrow thin stem blades and very short 0.25–0.5 mm collar hair curtain, versus a commonly longer fringe here. Compare D. commutatum for broad sometimes cordate stem-leaf bases and very short/absent ligule. Names such as Scribner's rosette-grass may occur under an infraspecific D. oligosanthes treatment; do not make a duplicate species card without taxon review.
